items.rationale: Independent review 2026-09-27 (lay reader and scientific reviewer): Lay reader: rarity stated as a fact about the arrangement, not about the reader's call; blood test phrase. Source said: You have the C282Y change on both copies of the HFE gene, with an extra H63D change on one of them. The HFE gene helps control how much iron the body absorbs from food. C282Y is the name lab reports use for a change of one DNA letter in the HFE gene that stops the protein it makes from working properly. H63D is the name lab reports use for a common one-letter change in the HFE gene whose effect on iron is small. This arrangement is very rare: expert guidelines state that the two changes arose separately in human history and are found on different copies of the gene. It is expected to work like having two C282Y copies, the pattern behind most hereditary haemochromatosis, because the extra change sits on a copy that is already affected; this has not been studied directly. By middle age most people with two C282Y copies have raised iron levels, and far fewer become ill, men much more often than women. A blood test of ferritin and transferrin saturation shows whether iron is building up, and a doctor decides what, if anything, to do. [jmc field=conclusion value_sha256=f51405ca3f62 source=PMIDs 26153218, 18199861 recorded=2026-09-27T08:02:06Z by=Anton Kulaga (with Claude)]

items.rationale: Independent review 2026-09-27 (lay reader and scientific reviewer): Scientific reviewer M5/C3: Allen 2008 disease definition includes raised liver enzymes, now said; added severe morbidity such as cirrhosis about 4% (5.6% in men), EMQN 2016 text located via fetch_fulltext; added siblings ~25% (EMQN) and that the usual treatment for high iron is simple and prevents damage (EMQN, AASLD), with a doctor deciding. Lay reader: blood test named as 'a blood test of iron levels (ferritin and transferrin saturation)'. Source said: You have two copies of the HFE change known as C282Y, one from each parent. The HFE gene helps control how much iron the body absorbs from food. C282Y is the name lab reports use for a change of one DNA letter in the HFE gene that stops the protein it makes from working properly. This is the pattern found in most people diagnosed with hereditary haemochromatosis, where the body slowly stores too much iron, and about 1 in 200 people of northern European ancestry have it. It is well established that by middle age most people with it have higher iron levels in the blood than people with two normal copies. Far fewer become ill: in a large study following people from middle age for about 12 years, about 28 in 100 men and 1 in 100 women with this result developed iron-related disease, such as liver damage or joint damage in the knuckles. Women are thought to be protected partly by monthly blood loss. A blood test of ferritin and transferrin saturation shows whether iron is building up, and a doctor decides what, if anything, to do. [jmc field=conclusion value_sha256=ffa14ef5fa90 source=PMIDs 18199861, 26153218, 21452290 recorded=2026-09-27T08:02:06Z by=Anton Kulaga (with Claude)]

items.rationale: Independent review 2026-09-27 (lay reader and scientific reviewer): Scientific reviewer M4: removed "(in trans), so neither copy makes the usual HFE protein" (H63D only changes the protein slightly); now says one copy carries C282Y which stops the protein working, the other H63D which changes it only slightly. Lay reader: "copy of the gene" not "copy of the chromosome"; removed the closing contrast with the cis result (planted doubt); blood test phrase. Source said: You have one C282Y change and one H63D change in the HFE gene, one on each copy of the chromosome (in trans), so neither copy makes the usual HFE protein. The HFE gene helps control how much iron the body absorbs from food. C282Y is the name lab reports use for a change of one DNA letter in the HFE gene that stops the protein it makes from working properly. H63D is the name lab reports use for a common one-letter change in the HFE gene whose effect on iron is small. Your iron levels are likely to run somewhat higher than those of people with two normal copies, but illness from iron is rare: in a large study following people from middle age for about 12 years, 1 of 82 men and none of 95 women with this combination developed iron-related disease. When people with it do build up too much iron, it is usually mild to moderate and usually comes with something else, such as heavy drinking or a fatty liver. About 2 in 100 people of northern European ancestry have this combination. A blood test of ferritin and transferrin saturation shows how your body is handling iron, and a doctor decides what, if anything, to do. This is a different finding from carrying both changes on the same copy, which leaves one normal copy.
